analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to cover their workers and families or pay into a new public health insurance plan, moving the country toward universal coverage.
analysis.headline: The HealthAmerica universal health care bill got Senate hearings but never a vote: it sat in the Senate Finance Committee from June 1991 until the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required nearly every employer to either enroll its full-time workers and their families in a health plan meeting federal standards, or pay a share of wages into a new public insurance program called AmeriCare. AmeriCare would cover uninsured children and pregnant women within two years and everyone not otherwise covered within seven. It also banned preexisting-condition exclusions, capped deductibles and out-of-pocket costs, guaranteed mental health benefits, gave small businesses tax credits, and created a federal board to negotiate down hospital and doctor prices.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and their families who had no health coverage or skimpy coverage, people with preexisting conditions who could be denied insurance, low-income families who would pay no premiums or cost-sharing, and small businesses that would get tax credits and access to Medicare-rate plans.

how_it_helps.text: Every employer must enroll full-time employees and their families in a qualifying health plan or pay a contribution toward their coverage under the new public plan, AmeriCare.
AmeriCare would provide basic health benefits to any child or pregnant woman without other coverage within two years, and to anyone still uncovered within seven years.
Health plans are barred from excluding or limiting coverage because of a preexisting condition.
Deductibles are capped at $250, copayments at 20%, and annual out-of-pocket expenses at $3,000, with no premiums or cost-sharing for families under the poverty line.

Plans must cover inpatient and outpatient hospital and physician care, diagnostic tests, prenatal and well-baby care, preventive services including pap smears and mammograms, and mental health care with minimum annual limits.
Small businesses get a tax credit for health plan costs, and self-employed people can deduct 100% of their health insurance cost instead of the 25% then allowed.

Businesses with fewer than 100 employees that did not offer coverage could buy private plans whose providers are paid at Medicare rates, and a Federal Health Expenditure Board would convene negotiations to set recommended provider payment rates to slow health cost inflation.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that do not provide qualifying plans would pay a set percentage of their wages into AmeriCare, facing civil penalties up to 15% of total wages for noncompliance; employees would pay limited premium shares through payroll withholding. Federal taxpayers fund the AmeriCare federal share, and hospitals seeing more public-program patients would see their Medicare disproportionate-share payments reduced.

drawbacks.text: Employers would bear a new payroll-based mandate or contribution, with penalties up to 15% of total wages for noncompliance — a real cost that small and medium firms lobbied hard against.

Medium-sized employers are not required to provide or contribute to coverage until the fifth year after enactment, and small employers until the sixth, with those deadlines tied to measured progress on uninsured workers — so full coverage would take years.
The bill preempts state laws that mandate benefits in covered plans and bars states from restricting managed care plans' selection of providers, weakening some state consumer protections.

Starting seven years after enactment, individuals must certify they have qualifying insurance to claim the personal tax exemption and to receive federal program benefits — an enforcement mechanism that falls on individuals.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This was one of the major universal-coverage proposals of the early 1990s: it would have extended guaranteed, affordable coverage to uninsured workers and their families while carving out long phase-ins and exemptions for small and medium businesses to blunt employer opposition. Its honest tradeoff is that employers pay substantially for the expansion, the public plan's cost-sharing was limited, and cost control relied on an untested negotiated-rate board. The main design criticism — that coverage would arrive slowly for the smallest firms — was deliberate, not accidental.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which held a series of hearings in Washington and in Michigan over two years, but the bill was never marked up or brought to the Senate floor, and it died when the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Sen. George Mitchell introduced the HealthAmerica Act on June 5, 1991, with Sens. Kennedy, Riegle, and Rockefeller joining as original sponsors, and it was referred to the Committee on Finance two days later.

Over the following fourteen months the Finance Committee's Subcommittee on Health for Families and the full Finance Committee held hearings, including field hearings in East Lansing and Muskegon, Michigan, with the hearings printed as Senate hearing records S.Hrg. 102-427, 102-462, 102-1050, and 102-1070.
The committee never reported the bill, no floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have owed new coverage or contribution payments, and health insurers whose plans would have faced community-rating and preexisting-condition rules, avoided all of it; the uninsured remained uninsured until the next reform attempt five years later.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and insurers that avoided new rules

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor on the record was a Democrat, and the bill died in committee without a floor vote in a Democratically controlled Senate, so no bipartisan coalition ever formed around it.

industries.industry: Employers, especially small and medium businesses
industries.note: The bill would have required employers to fund coverage or pay a share of wages into the public plan, with penalties up to 15% of wages. Business groups fought the mandate, which is why the bill delayed requirements for the smallest firms for five to six years.

The bill keeps employer-sponsored private insurance as the main coverage channel — guaranteeing insurers millions of new customers — while subjecting their small-group plans to new standards: guaranteed issue within community-rating limits, preexisting-condition rules, and regulated cost-sharing.

The bill sets national standards that preempt state laws restricting managed care plans' selection of providers and negotiation of rates, and requires every state's AmeriCare program to offer competitively selected managed care plans to enrollees.

A new Federal Health Expenditure Board would convene negotiations over recommended hospital and physician payment rates, and small-business plans could pay providers at Medicare rates — mechanisms providers resisted as government rate-setting, but which aimed to hold down what patients and the public pay.
